newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Firmer data cheers Bonn, leaves hope on EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Firmer data cheers Bonn, leaves hope on EMU.

text.p: Battling its worst post-war jobs crisis, the Bonn government on Thursday received improved economic news, raising hopes Germany may still manage to meet the deficit goal for Europe's currency union to the letter.

But the flipside to slightly stronger economic data is that it may prompt the inflation-conscious Bundesbank to raise interest rates sooner rather than later, a step sure to shock Europe as nations work feverishly to get their economies in shape to qualify for monetary union in 1999.

Although German unemployment, climbing to 4.7 million in February, remains stuck at the highest levels seen since the 1930s, the Labour Office sought to put a more positive spin on the news, forecasting a turnaround this summer.
"The government's forecast of 4.2 million average jobless in 1997 is not unrealistic," Labour Office president Bernhard Jagoda told a news conference.

Bonn officials, insisting Germany can still meet the Maastricht Treaty deficit goal, earlier based forecasts for a 2.9 percent 1997 budget deficit on this average jobless level -- a deficit level that would allow it to qualify.
Economists also welcomed news that January orders jumped 4.6 percent on the year, outpacing expectations and adding more weight to cautious predictions economic recovery may be on the horizon.
Higher January import and wholesale prices and fourth quarter 1996 gross domestic product earlier cheered markets.
"The growth outlook has improved and the government should find a way to come close to EMU targets," said Gernot Nerb, economist at Salomon Brothers in London.

In a meeting with Italian opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, the driving force behind European integration, again insisted the currency union's start date and entry criteria would not be changed.

To qualify for the currency union, nations must present low inflation and long-term interest rates, stable foreign exchange rates and budget discipline, not exceeding low reference values on budget deficits and government debt.
But Europe's unexpectedly deep recession wreaked fiscal havoc on a number of nations, including Germany, prompting draconian government measures to fulfil all the criteria.
Now economists say Germany is facing a particular dilemma as its record-high jobless rate makes it look that much worse when compared with Italy's considerable consolidation efforts.

"The more Italy's finances improve and the higher Germany's jobless rate remains, the more difficult it will be for Germany to keep Italy out of the currency union," said one analyst, asking not to be identified.
But he added: "Italy's entry would make it difficult to convince German citizens the new euro will be as strong as the mark."

German officials have sought to soothe ruffled Italian feathers over the EMU entry issue stressing they would welcome as many nations as possible in the union as long as these nations meet all criteria, ensuring a stable currency union.

Meanwhile the stronger data may however create problems for Bonn as the Bundesbank may feel compelled to take preventative action, beating back renewed inflationary pressures with a rate hike, possibly even before year-end.

"There is still a window of opportunity for a rate hike in the fourth quarter 1997", said Joachim Fels, economist at Morgan Stanley in London, stressing, however, the Bundesbank would then act only if inflation accelerated past two percent.

Other economists agreed that inflation, while not a problem at present, remained the Bundesbank's chief worry, particularly as the Bundesbank prepares to hand over its monetary reins to the European Central Bank boasting low inflation levels.
Consequently the U.S. dollar has moved into the spotlight as the key influence for German rates as its strength could quickly translate into higher German inflation rates, economists said.

But a rate hike could be extremely difficult politically as it could be misinterpreted to mean the Bundesbank were trying to unhinge Europe's currency union goals, said Thomas Mayer, economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt.
Thus the Bundesbank "will not be in a position to raise interest rates until every last person realises such a step would not be taken to endanger the timely start of monetary union," he argued.
